MarmotMeshfreeCore

class Approximation
#include <MarmotMeshfreeApproximation.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Approximation:

Abstract interface of a meshfree approximation, which evaluates shape functions from a set of kernels.

Given an evaluation point \( \boldsymbol{x} \) and a list of \( n \) candidate kernel functions \( \phi_A \), \( A = 0, \dots, n-1 \) (KernelFunction), an approximation computes the shape functions \( \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) \) and/or their gradients. The output arrays are indexed by the position of the kernel in the candidate list; candidates that do not cover \( \boldsymbol{x} \) get zero entries.

The gradient output is a column-major \( d \times n \) array, i.e., entry \( i + d\,A \) holds \( \partial \Psi_A / \partial x_i \), where \( d \) is the spatial dimension.

Subclassed by Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximation

template<int nDim, int order>
class BSplineCellGeometry : public Marmot::Discretizations::Elements::BSplineGeometryElement<nDim, order>
#include <MarmotBSplineCellGeometry.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::BSplineCellGeometry:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::BSplineCellGeometry:

B-spline cell geometry (one knot span), a geometry policy for the MPM cells.

Wraps Marmot::Discretizations::Elements::BSplineGeometryElement for use as the GeometryCell of a cell (see GeometryCellPolicy). The cell is the knot span \( [u_{p}, u_{p+1}] \) of each direction; the knot vectors are given in physical coordinates, so the parametric coordinate of a point is the point itself: findReferenceCoordinate() is the identity and dNdX() returns the parametric derivatives unchanged. This is exact for a B-spline grid whose geometry map is the identity \( \boldsymbol{X}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \boldsymbol{\xi} \) (control points at the Greville abscissae, e.g. a uniform, axis-aligned background grid); the control point coordinates enter only detJ().

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – Spatial dimension (2 or 3).

  • order – Polynomial degree \( p \) (1, 2 or 3 are registered).

template<int nDim, int order>
class BSplineGeometryElement
#include <MarmotBSplineGeometryElement.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Elements::BSplineGeometryElement:

Geometry of a single knot span of a tensor-product B-spline of degree order.

The element is one knot span \( [u_p, u_{p+1}] \) per direction of a B-spline of degree \( p \) = order. The \( p+1 \) basis functions that are nonzero on that span depend on the \( 2p+2 \) knots \( u_0,\dots,u_{2p+1} \) of each direction, which are passed to the constructor. The shape functions are tensor products of the univariate B-splines \( B_{i,p} \) (Cox–de Boor recursion, see MarmotBSpline.h),

\[ N_{a}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = B_{i,p}(\xi_1)\,B_{j,p}(\xi_2)\,B_{k,p}(\xi_3), \qquad a = i + j\,(p+1) + k\,(p+1)^2 , \]
i.e. with the index of the first direction running fastest. The parametric coordinates \( \boldsymbol{\xi} \) are the knot values themselves (the normalization of the knot vectors to \( [-1,1] \) is disabled, so _knotVectorsNormalized is a copy of _knotVectors).

Note

Only 2D and 3D are usable: in 1D, the constructor throws for order > 1 (no shape with \( p+1 > 2 \) nodes in 1D), and dNdXi() would not compile if instantiated.

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – Spatial dimension (2 or 3).

  • order – Polynomial degree \( p \) of the B-spline.

Subclassed by Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::BSplineCellGeometry< nDim, order >

class Cell
#include <MarmotCell.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::Cell:

Abstract interface of a background cell of the material point method (MPM).

A cell is a fixed background element with \( n_\mathrm{nodes} \) nodes that carries the nodal fields (e.g. the displacement) and the interpolation \( N_A(\boldsymbol{X}) \). It does not own any quadrature points: in every connectivity update, the host framework assigns to each cell the material points (Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint) that currently lie inside it, and the cell integrates over those material points, e.g. for the internal force

\[ \boldsymbol{f}^{\mathrm{int}}_A = \sum_{p \in \text{cell}} \boldsymbol{f}_{A}(\text{MP}_p)\,V_p , \]
with the material point volume \( V_p \). The concrete kernel (which stress, which volume, which configuration) is defined by the implementing cell, see e.g. Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::DisplacementCell.

Dof layout. The cell vectors (Q, fInt, fExt) have getNDofPerCell() entries, the matrices are dense with getNDofPerCell() \( \times \) getNDofPerCell() entries. getNodeFields() lists for each node the names of the fields it carries; getDofIndicesPermutationPattern() is the permutation that maps the node-major dof order of the host framework to the cell-internal order (for the cells in Marmot: blocked, i.e. all dofs of the first field, then all dofs of the second field; within a field node-major, component fastest).

Call sequence of the host framework (e.g. EdelweissMeshfree), per time increment:

  1. Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint::prepareYourself() on all material points,

  2. isCoordinateInCell() / getBoundingBox() to find the cells hit by the material points, then assignMaterialPoints() on every active cell (connectivity update),

  3. in every Newton iteration: Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint::prepareYourself() (resets the accumulated increment), interpolateFieldsToMaterialPoints() on all active cells, Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint::computeYourself() on all material points, then computeMaterialPointKernels(), computeBodyLoad(), computeDistributedLoad() (and the inertia methods for dynamic analyses) on all active cells,

  4. after convergence, Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint::acceptStateAndPosition() on all material points.

Instances are created by name via Marmot::Registry::CellFactory.

Subclassed by Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::CellElement

class CellElement : public Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::Cell
#include <MarmotCellElement.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::CellElement:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::CellElement:

A Cell that defines its own material points, like a finite element defines its quadrature points.

In contrast to a plain Cell, which integrates over whatever material points currently lie inside it, a cell element requests a fixed set of material points: the host framework queries getNMaterialPoints(), getRequestedMaterialPointCoordinates() and getRequestedMaterialPointVolumes(), creates one material point per request (e.g. at the points of the quadrature rule passed to Marmot::Registry::CellElementFactory), and assigns them back with Cell::assignMaterialPoints(). The cell element may additionally carry its own state variables.

Instances are created by name via Marmot::Registry::CellElementFactory. No concrete cell element is contained in Marmot at present.

template<int nDim>
class GenericParticle : public Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Particle
#include <GenericParticle.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericParticle:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericParticle:

Common base of the point particles (one evaluation point at the particle center), independent of the physics.

GenericParticle implements the parts of the Particle interface that do not depend on the physics:

  • the geometry of a point particle: a single vertex at the center \( \boldsymbol{Y}_c \) in the reference intermediate configuration (the last accepted configuration), shape “point”;

  • the shape functions: assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions() evaluates the trial functions \( N_A \) and their gradients \( \partial N_A / \partial Y_i \) at the center (direct nodal integration); the test functions \( T_A \), \( \partial T_A / \partial Y_i \) start as copies of them (Bubnov-Galerkin) and are changed only by the VCI correction (Petrov-Galerkin). Derived classes (e.g., the SQCNI particles) may replace the gradients by smoothed ones;

  • the property “VCI order” and the particle contributions to the variationally consistent integration (VCI) of Chen, Hillman and Rüter (2013).

VCI. For the VCI order \( k \), the basis \( \boldsymbol{P}(\boldsymbol{Y}) \) is the complete monomial basis of degree \( \le k \) in \( n_{\text{dim}} \) variables (Math::computeMonomialBasis()), with \( n_C = \binom{k + n_{\text{dim}}}{n_{\text{dim}}} \) entries, evaluated at the particle center. With the particle volume \( V_Y \) in the reference intermediate configuration as the integration weight, the particle contributes

\[ \int \partial_i T_A\, P_C \,dV \approx \partial_i T_A\, P_C\, V_Y, \qquad \int T_A\, \partial_i P_C \,dV \approx T_A\, \partial_i P_C\, V_Y, \qquad M_{ACD} \approx \chi_A\, P_C\, P_D\, V_Y, \]
where \( \chi_A \in \{0, 1\} \) indicates whether the particle center is in the support of kernel function \( A \). The correction assigned by vci_assignTestFunctionCorrectionTerms() is \( \partial_i T_A \mathrel{+}= \chi_A \sum_C \eta_{AiC} P_C \). The boundary integral depends on the kinematics of the physics and is left to the derived classes.

Derived classes must keep _centerReferenceIntermediate, _volReferenceIntermediate, _P and _P_Gradient up to date in acceptStateAndPosition().

nDim – The number of dimensions (2 or 3).

template<int nDim, int nVertices>
class GenericSDIParticle : public Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Particle
#include <GenericSDIParticle.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericSDIParticle:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericSDIParticle:

A generic, physics-independent base class for particles with subdomain integration (SDI).

The particle domain (a ParticleDomain, e.g., a quadrilateral or a hexahedron) is uniformly subdivided once into \( 2^{n_{\text{dim}}} \) subdomains (ParticleDomain::uniformSubdivided()). Each subdomain \( s \) is an integration point of its own: the derived class attaches a material point to it and integrates the weak form as a sum over the subdomains. The shape functions of a subdomain are evaluated at its center, and their gradients are smoothed over its smoothing domain \( \Omega_s \) by the divergence theorem, with one point (the face center \( \boldsymbol{Y}_f \)) per face \( f \) and the boundary surface vector \( \boldsymbol{n}_f\,dA_f \),

\[ \frac{\partial N_A}{\partial Y_i}\bigg|_s \approx \frac{1}{|\Omega_s|} \sum_f N_A(\boldsymbol{Y}_f)\, n_{f,i}\, dA_f \]
(see _smoothDerivativeShapeFunctionsForParticleDomain()). The test functions start as copies of the trial functions and are changed only by the VCI correction.

The particle as a whole moves with its center: in computePhysicsKernels(), the displacement increment and the deformation gradient increment of the center are computed from the shape functions of the main domain,

\[ \Delta\boldsymbol{u}_c = \sum_B N_B\, \Delta\boldsymbol{q}_B, \qquad \Delta\boldsymbol{F}_c = \boldsymbol{I} + \sum_B \Delta\boldsymbol{q}_B \otimes \frac{\partial N_B}{\partial \boldsymbol{Y}}, \]
and in acceptStateAndPosition() the total central deformation gradient \( \boldsymbol{F}_c \leftarrow \Delta\boldsymbol{F}_c\, \boldsymbol{F}_c \) and the total center displacement \( \boldsymbol{u}_c \) move the main domain and all subdomains (ParticleDomain::acceptStateAndPosition()).

State variable layout. The block given to assignStateVars() is

offset

size

content

0

nDim

center displacement \( \boldsymbol{u}_c \)

nDim

nDim * nDim

central deformation gradient \( \boldsymbol{F}_c \) (column-major)

nDim + nDim * nDim

nDim * nDim

its increment \( \Delta\boldsymbol{F}_c \) (column-major)

…

the states of the subdomains (derived class)

The center block of nStateVarsCenter doubles is padded to a multiple of 8 doubles (64 bytes), and derived classes pad the block of every subdomain in the same way (paddedStateVarSize()), so that each subdomain block starts at a multiple of 8 doubles from the start of the particle block.

Derived classes implement the physics on the subdomains (the …OnSubdomains() methods, getSubdomainVolume(), the loads and the VCI boundary integral).

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – The number of dimensions (2 or 3).

  • nVertices – The number of vertices defining the particle’s geometry (4 or 8).

virtual void computePhysicsKernels(const double *dQ, double *fInt, double *dFInt_ddQ, double timeNew, double dT) final override

Computes the physics kernels (internal forces and their derivatives) for the particle.

Updates the center kinematics from the main domain (the center displacement is incremented by \( \sum_B N_B \Delta\boldsymbol{q}_B \) and \( \Delta\boldsymbol{F}_c \) is set, see the class documentation), then calls computePhysicsKernelsOnSubdomains(). As for all Marmot entities, the state variables are updated in place, and the host restores them to the last accepted state before each evaluation (EdelweissMeshfree does so in every computePhysicsKernels call): the center displacement thus stays the total one, which acceptStateAndPosition() applies to the undeformed domain.

Parameters:

  • dQ – [in] Incremental nodal displacements (the first nDim dofs of each node are used).

  • fInt – [inout] Internal force vector.

  • dFInt_ddQ – [inout] Stiffness matrix (derivative of internal forces with respect to incremental displacements).

  • timeNew – [in] The current simulation time.

  • dT – [in] The time step size.

static inline constexpr int paddedStateVarSize(int n)

The size of a block of state variables, rounded up to a multiple of 8 doubles (64 bytes).

The blocks of the particle itself and of every subdomain start at such a multiple, so that the state of each subdomain is aligned as the state of a stand-alone material point: Fastor may use aligned SIMD stores on the tensor maps into it (seen with GCC 14.2 -O3, a segmentation fault for a block starting at an odd double). The offsets are relative to the start of the particle’s block, so the absolute alignment also requires the host framework to pass an aligned block.

Parameters:

n – [in] The unpadded number of state variables.

Returns:

n rounded up to a multiple of 8.

class KernelFunction
#include <MarmotMeshfreeKernelFunction.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunction:

Abstract interface of a meshfree kernel (window) function \( \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) \).

A kernel function is attached to a node (particle) \( A \) with center \( \boldsymbol{x}_A \) and has compact support. The reproducing kernel approximation (ReproducingKernelApproximation) builds its shape functions \( \Psi_A \) by correcting these kernels such that polynomials up to a given order are reproduced exactly; the continuity of \( \Psi_A \) is inherited from the kernel.

All coordinates are passed as raw arrays of length \( d \) (the spatial dimension of the kernel). The configuration in which the coordinates are given (reference or current) is decided by the caller; the kernel only compares them with its center coordinates.

Subclassed by Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline2ndOrderBoxed, Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline3rdOrderBoxed

class KernelFunctionBSpline2ndOrderBoxed : public Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunction
#include <MarmotMeshfreeKernelFunctionBSpline2ndOrderBoxed.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline2ndOrderBoxed:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline2ndOrderBoxed:

Boxed tensor-product kernel from 2nd order (quadratic) B-splines.

The kernel of node \( A \) with center \( \boldsymbol{x}_A \) and support radius \( a \) is the tensor product of one-dimensional 2nd order (quadratic) B-splines \( w \) in each coordinate direction,

\[ \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} w\left( x_i - x_{A,i} \right), \]
with
\[\begin{split} w(r) = \begin{cases} 1 - 2 z^2, & 0 \le z \le \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ 2 (1 - z)^2, & \tfrac{1}{2} < z \le 1, \\ 0, & z > 1, \end{cases} \qquad z = \frac{|r|}{a}. \end{split}\]
\( w \) is the quadratic B-spline on the knots \( \{-a, -a/2, a/2, a\} \), scaled to \( w(0) = 1 \); it is \( C^1 \)-continuous, so the kernel and the resulting reproducing kernel shape functions are \( C^1 \).

The support is the open box \( |x_i - x_{A,i}| < a \), \( i = 1, \dots, d \) (hence “boxed”); its bounding box is \( [\boldsymbol{x}_A - a, \boldsymbol{x}_A + a] \). The support radius \( a \) is the half edge length of the box, identical in all directions, and the kernel is not normalized (the reproducing kernel correction removes any constant scaling of the kernel).

Note

The kernel does not own its center coordinates: it stores the pointer passed to the constructor, and moveTo() writes the new center through this pointer. The pointed-to storage must outlive the kernel.

  • supportRadius – [in] Support radius \( a \).

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline3rdOrderBoxed:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::KernelFunctionBSpline3rdOrderBoxed:

Boxed tensor-product kernel from 3rd order (cubic) B-splines.

The kernel of node \( A \) with center \( \boldsymbol{x}_A \) and support radius \( a \) is the tensor product of one-dimensional 3rd order (cubic) B-splines \( w \) in each coordinate direction,

\[ \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} w\left( x_i - x_{A,i} \right), \]
with
\[\begin{split} w(r) = \begin{cases} \tfrac{2}{3} - 4 z^2 + 4 z^3, & 0 \le z \le \tfrac{1}{2}, \\ \tfrac{4}{3} (1 - z)^3, & \tfrac{1}{2} < z \le 1, \\ 0, & z > 1, \end{cases} \qquad z = \frac{|r|}{a}. \end{split}\]
\( w \) is the standard cubic B-spline on the uniform knots \( \{-a, -a/2, 0, a/2, a\} \) (knot spacing \( a/2 \), \( w(0) = 2/3 \)); it is \( C^2 \)-continuous, so the kernel and the resulting reproducing kernel shape functions are \( C^2 \).

The support is the open box \( |x_i - x_{A,i}| < a \), \( i = 1, \dots, d \) (hence “boxed”); its bounding box is \( [\boldsymbol{x}_A - a, \boldsymbol{x}_A + a] \). The support radius \( a \) is the half edge length of the box, identical in all directions, and the kernel is not normalized (the reproducing kernel correction removes any constant scaling of the kernel).

Note

The kernel does not own its center coordinates: it stores the pointer passed to the constructor, and moveTo() writes the new center through this pointer. The pointed-to storage must outlive the kernel.

template<int nDim, int nNodes>
class LagrangeCell
#include <MarmotMeshfreeQuadHexCell.h>

Generic isoparametric Lagrange element.

This class provides common functionality for isoparametric elements, including mapping from natural to physical coordinates, Jacobian computation, and integration-based properties like centroid and volume.

Specific shape functions and derivatives must be specialized for concrete topologies. Specializations exist for Quad4 (2, 4) and Hex8 (3, 8). The class owns a copy of the node coordinates (unlike the MPM cell geometries, which map an external array); it is used as the geometry of particle domains (see MarmotParticleDomain.h).

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – The dimension of the element (e.g., 2 for Quad4, 3 for Hex8).

  • nNodes – The number of nodes in the element (e.g., 4 for Quad4, 8 for Hex8).

template<int nDim, int nNodes>
class LagrangianCellGeometry : public Marmot::Discretizations::Elements::GeometryElement<nDim, nNodes>
#include <MarmotLagrangianCellGeometry.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::LagrangianCellGeometry:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::LagrangianCellGeometry:

Isoparametric Lagrangian cell geometry (Quad4, Hexa8), a geometry policy for the MPM cells.

Uses the shape functions \( N_A(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \), \( \boldsymbol{\xi}\in[-1,1]^{n_\mathrm{dim}} \), of Marmot::Discretizations::Elements::GeometryElement and the isoparametric map \( \boldsymbol{X}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) = \sum_A N_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\boldsymbol{X}_A \) with the nodal coordinates \( \boldsymbol{X}_A \), and provides the inverse map, the physical gradients and the point location test required by GeometryCellPolicy.

For axis-aligned rectangular (box-shaped) cells, the inverse map findReferenceCoordinate() and the point location test isCoordinateInCell() are exact and cheap (affine map of the bounding box); for distorted cells, the inverse map is computed by Newton’s method, and the point location test uses it.

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – Spatial dimension (2 or 3).

  • nNodes – Number of nodes (4 in 2D, 8 in 3D).

Public Types

bool isCoordinateInCell(const double *coordinates) const

Point location test: bounding box test \( X_{\min,i} \le x_i < X_{\max,i} \), and for a distorted cell additionally \( -1 \le \xi_i < 1 \) for the parametric coordinates of findReferenceCoordinate().

Both tests are half-open, so that a point on a face shared by two cells belongs to exactly one of them; consequently, a point exactly on the upper boundary of the whole mesh belongs to no cell.

coordinates – [in] Point coordinates (nDim values).

Returns:

true if the point is inside the cell.

Inverse isoparametric map \( \boldsymbol{\xi}(\boldsymbol{X}) \).

Starts from the affine map of the bounding box, \( \xi_i = 2\,(X_i - \tfrac12(X_{\max,i}+X_{\min,i}))/(X_{\max,i}-X_{\min,i}) \), which is exact for an axis-aligned box-shaped cell, and applies Newton’s method, \( \boldsymbol{\xi} \leftarrow \boldsymbol{\xi} + \boldsymbol{J}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{X} - \sum_A N_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\boldsymbol{X}_A) \), until the residual is below \( 10^{-12} \) times the diagonal of the bounding box.

class MaterialPoint
#include <MarmotMaterialPoint.h>

Abstract interface of a material point of the material point method (MPM).

A material point is a Lagrangian integration point that carries mass (volume and density), position and the complete history (deformation, stress, material state variables) through the simulation, while the background cells (Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::Cell) carry the nodal fields and are reset every increment. A material point owns its constitutive model (assigned with assignMaterial()); its state variables live in an externally owned array (assigned with assignStateVars()).

Life cycle (as called by the host framework, e.g. EdelweissMeshfree):

  1. creation by name via Marmot::Registry::MaterialPointFactory, then assignMaterial(), getNumberOfRequiredStateVars() and assignStateVars(),

  2. initializeYourself() once, before the first increment,

  3. per iteration: prepareYourself(), then the cells interpolate the nodal increments to the material point (Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::Cell::interpolateFieldsToMaterialPoints()), then computeYourself(), which evaluates the constitutive response that the cells integrate in Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::Cell::computeMaterialPointKernels(),

  4. acceptStateAndPosition() after convergence of the increment, which commits the increment (e.g. updates position and deformation gradient).

State contract: the state variable array is a trial copy. Before every iteration (i.e. before prepareYourself()), the host restores it to the values committed by the last acceptStateAndPosition(), and the cells interpolate the total increment since that state (not the Newton correction). Implementations may therefore update their state in place during an iteration (e.g. add the interpolated increment of a field to its committed value), since each iteration starts again from the committed state; a cutback is simply a restore. EdelweissMeshfree implements this by copying the committed array into the trial array in prepareYourself() and back in acceptStateAndPosition().

The kinematic update from the cell (e.g. incrementDeformation) and the response/tangent quantities read by the cell are not part of this interface: they are specific to each pair of concrete cell and material point (see e.g. Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::DisplacementMaterialPoint), and the cell obtains them by a dynamic_cast.

class MaterialPointFactory
#include <MarmotMPMLibrary.h>

Registry of Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint types, created by name.

A material point module registers each of its types once, at static initialization time, with a factory function (typically a captureless lambda) in its *Registration.cpp: 

const static bool isRegistered = Marmot::Registry::MaterialPointFactory::registerMaterialPoint(
"Displacement/PlaneStrain",
  []( int n, const double* coords, int sizeCoords, double volume ) ->
Marmot::Discretizations::MaterialPoints::MaterialPoint* { return new DisplacementMaterialPoint2D( n, coords,
sizeCoords, volume ); } );
Names are case-insensitive (stored in upper case). The class is not instantiable; all members are static.

class Particle
#include <MarmotParticle.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Particle:

Abstract interface of a particle of the reproducing kernel particle method (RKPM).

A particle is the integration entity of the meshfree layer: it represents a piece of the body (its domain, commonly a point, a quadrilateral or a hexahedron) and it evaluates the weak form on that piece. Unlike a finite element, a particle has no fixed nodes. It interacts with the degrees of freedom, which live on the nodes of the meshfree kernel functions (KernelFunction), via the shape functions of a meshfree approximation (Approximation). The host framework (e.g., EdelweissMeshfree) finds the kernel functions whose support covers the particle and hands them over with assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions(); the particle then evaluates the shape functions \( N_A \) and (possibly smoothed) gradients \( \partial N_A / \partial Y \) of these \( A = 1 \dots n_{\text{nodes}} \) nodes.

Similar to finite elements, a particle computes the internal forces and their derivatives (computePhysicsKernels()), body loads (computeBodyLoad()) and distributed loads (computeDistributedLoad()). Concrete particles work in an updated Lagrangian setting: gradients are taken with respect to the coordinates \( Y \) of the last accepted (reference intermediate) configuration, and acceptStateAndPosition() moves the particle to the new configuration at the end of a converged increment.

A typical life cycle driven by the host framework is

  1. creation via Marmot::Registry::ParticleFactory::createParticle(),

  2. setProperties() (e.g., the order of the variationally consistent integration and time integration parameters),

  3. assignStateVars() with a block of getNumberOfRequiredStateVars() doubles, initializeYourself(),

  4. per increment: assignMeshfreeKernelFunctions(), optionally the VCI methods (vci_…), then repeatedly computePhysicsKernels() and the load methods, and after convergence acceptStateAndPosition().

State contract: the state variable block is a trial copy. Before every call of computePhysicsKernels(), the host restores it to the values committed by the last acceptStateAndPosition(), and dQ is the total increment since that state (not the Newton correction). Implementations may therefore update their state in place during computePhysicsKernels() (e.g. add the increment of the center displacement or of a nonlocal field to its committed value, or integrate velocities and accelerations), since every call starts again from the committed state; a cutback is simply a restore. EdelweissMeshfree implements this by copying the committed block into the trial block before each computePhysicsKernels() and back in acceptStateAndPosition().

For the residual vector and the stiffness matrix, unlike elements and cells, no (field-)blocked layout is possible. This is due to the fact that the number of nodes per particle is not fixed and may vary, and accordingly, the dofIndicesPermutationPattern used to designate the structure of a blocked storage may vary. Accordingly, for performance reasons, no dofIndicesPermutationPattern is provided, and the residual vector and the stiffness matrix are computed in a non-blocked, node-wise layout. Example: [node_1_displacement, node_1_temperature, node_2_displacement, node_2_temperature, …], in which nodes designate the nodes of the kernel functions attached to the particle, in the order in which they were assigned. The size of both is thus \( n_{\text{nodes}} \cdot \) getNBaseDof().

For the stiffness matrix, a column-major layout is used.

The particle also offers the local contributions to the variationally consistent integration (VCI) of Chen, Hillman and Rüter (2013), see the vci_… methods. The global assembly and solution of the VCI correction is done by the host framework.

Subclassed by Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericParticle< nDim >, Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::GenericSDIParticle< nDim, nVertices >

Variationally consistent integration (VCI)

The VCI method of Chen, Hillman and Rüter (2013) corrects the gradients of the test functions, \( \partial T_A / \partial Y_i = \partial N_A / \partial Y_i + \chi_A \sum_C \eta_{AiC}\, P_C \), such that the integration by parts is exact under the numerical integration for a polynomial basis \( P_C(Y) \) (the complete monomials up to the VCI order); \( \chi_A \) is the indicator of the support of kernel function \( A \),

\[ \int_\Omega \frac{\partial T_A}{\partial Y_i} P_C \, dV + \int_\Omega T_A \frac{\partial P_C}{\partial Y_i} \, dV = \int_{\partial\Omega} T_A P_C n_i \, dA . \]
The particles provide their local contributions to these integrals, all arrays are row-major, sized \( n_{\text{nodes}} \times n_{\text{dim}} \times n_C \) (index \( AiC \)) or \( n_{\text{nodes}} \times n_C \times n_C \) (index \( ACD \)), and contributions are accumulated (+=). The host framework assembles them over all particles per node \( A \) and solves \( \sum_D M_{ACD}\, \eta_{AiD} = R_{AiC} \) with the residual \( R_{AiC} = \int_{\partial\Omega} T_A P_C n_i\,dA - \int_\Omega \partial_i T_A\, P_C\,dV - \int_\Omega T_A\, \partial_i P_C\,dV \).

template<int nDim, int nVertices>
class ParticleDomain
#include <MarmotParticleDomain.h>

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ParticleDomain:

The geometry of a cell-shaped particle, independent of physics or meshfree approximation.

A particle domain is a Lagrangian cell (LagrangeCell, e.g., a 4-node quadrilateral or an 8-node hexahedron) that is kept in three versions:

  • the undeformed geometry with the vertices \( \boldsymbol{X}_v \) and the centroid \( \boldsymbol{X}_c \) given at construction,

  • the deformed geometry (the geometry in the reference intermediate configuration, i.e., the last accepted configuration), used for the particle position, the face centers, the boundary surface vectors of distributed loads and the second moments of the NSNI stabilization,

  • the smoothing domain, over whose boundary the smoothed shape function gradients are integrated (see GenericSDIParticle and the SQCNI particles).

Both deformed versions are obtained from the undeformed geometry by a homogeneous deformation about the centroid plus the displacement of the center (see acceptStateAndPosition()),

\[ \boldsymbol{x}_v = \boldsymbol{X}_c + \boldsymbol{F}\,(\boldsymbol{X}_v - \boldsymbol{X}_c) + \boldsymbol{u}_c , \]
where \( \boldsymbol{X}_c \) is the centroid of the particle; for the subdomains of uniformSubdivided() it is the centroid of the parent domain, so that the subdomains remain a tiling of the deformed parent. with the total deformation gradient \( \boldsymbol{F} \) of the particle for the deformed geometry, and a tensor \( \boldsymbol{F}_s \) derived from it according to SmoothingDomainUpdateType for the smoothing domain. Face IDs are 1-based and follow the Abaqus convention of LagrangeCell.

Template Parameters:

  • nDim – The number of dimensions (2 or 3).

  • nVertices – The number of vertices of the cell (4 for a quadrilateral, 8 for a hexahedron).

Public Types

enum SmoothingDomainUpdateType

Defines how the smoothing domain follows the deformation of the particle.

The smoothing domain is mapped with the tensor \( \boldsymbol{F}_s \) computed by _computeSmoothingDomainDeformationTensorTotal(); in all cases it is translated by the center displacement. The registered particle names encode the choice (e.g., SQCNI: DeformationGradient, SNNI: None, suffix _R or prefix R-: RotationOnly, suffix _RU or prefix RS-: RotationAndPrincipalStretch).

Values:

enumerator None

\( \boldsymbol{F}_s = \boldsymbol{I} \): the smoothing domain keeps its undeformed shape and is only translated.

enumerator DeformationGradient

\( \boldsymbol{F}_s = \boldsymbol{F} \): the smoothing domain deforms with the particle (it coincides with the deformed geometry).

enumerator RotationOnly

\( \boldsymbol{F}_s = \boldsymbol{R} \), the rotation of the polar decomposition \( \boldsymbol{F} = \boldsymbol{R}\boldsymbol{U} \) (from an SVD).

enumerator RotationAndPrincipalStretch

\( \boldsymbol{F}_s = \boldsymbol{R}\,\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{R}^T < \boldsymbol{F}) \): the rotation and the diagonal entries of \( \boldsymbol{U} \) in the global basis.

class ParticleFactory
#include <MarmotParticleLibrary.h>

Registry and factory of the meshfree particles (Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Particle).

  • Allows particles to register themselves with their name (see registerParticle(); particle modules do this in their *Registration.cpp files at static initialization).

  • Allows the user (the host framework) to create instances of particles by name (createParticle()).

Particle names are case-insensitive: they are converted to upper case both at registration and at creation. They follow the pattern <Physics><IntegrationScheme>/<Dimension>/<Shape>, e.g., DisplacementSQCNI/PlaneStrain/Quad or GradientEnhancedFiniteStrainSQCNIxNSNI/3D/Hexa.

class ReproducingKernelApproximation : public Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::Approximation
#include <MarmotMeshfreeReproducingKernelApproximation.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximation:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximation:

Reproducing kernel (RK) approximation with explicit (direct) shape function gradients.

The shape function of node \( A \) is the kernel \( \phi_A \) (KernelFunction) multiplied by a correction function,

\[ \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}^T(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A)\, \boldsymbol{b}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}), \]
where \( \boldsymbol{H} \) is the vector of all monomials up to the completeness order \( n \) (Math::computeMonomialBasis(), first entry \( 1 \)) evaluated at the shifted coordinates \( \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A \). The coefficient vector \( \boldsymbol{b} \) solves
\[ \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{b}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}_0, \qquad \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_{B} \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B)\, \boldsymbol{H}^T(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B)\, \phi_B(\boldsymbol{x}), \qquad \boldsymbol{H}_0 = \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{0}) = [1, 0, \dots, 0]^T, \]
with the moment matrix \( \boldsymbol{M} \) summed over the kernels covering \( \boldsymbol{x} \). This enforces the reproducing conditions \( \sum_A \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x})\, (\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A)^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \delta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{0}} \), or equivalently \( \sum_A \Psi_A(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{x}_A^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \boldsymbol{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \), for all multi-indices \( |\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le n \); in particular, the shape functions form a partition of unity. The continuity of \( \Psi_A \) is that of the kernels.

The gradients are the exact derivatives of \( \Psi_A \) (product rule),

\[ \Psi_{A,i} = \left( \boldsymbol{b}_{,i}^T \boldsymbol{H} + \boldsymbol{b}^T \boldsymbol{H}_{,i} \right) \phi_A + \boldsymbol{b}^T \boldsymbol{H}\, \phi_{A,i}, \qquad \boldsymbol{b}_{,i} = -\boldsymbol{M}^{-1} \boldsymbol{M}_{,i}\, \boldsymbol{b}, \qquad \boldsymbol{M}_{,i} = \sum_B \left( \boldsymbol{H}_{,i} \boldsymbol{H}^T + \boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{H}_{,i}^T \right) \phi_B + \boldsymbol{H} \boldsymbol{H}^T \phi_{B,i}, \]
with \( (\bullet)_{,i} = \partial (\bullet) / \partial x_i \) and \( \boldsymbol{H} \) evaluated at \( \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A \) (resp. \( \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_B \)). The linear systems are solved with a column-pivoting Householder QR decomposition of \( \boldsymbol{M} \), which is computed once per evaluation point.

If fewer kernels cover \( \boldsymbol{x} \) than the basis has entries, \( \boldsymbol{M} \) is singular; the completeness order is then reduced for this evaluation point (getCorrectedCompletenessOrder()).

See ReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit for the variant with implicit gradients.

Eigen::ColPivHouseholderQR<Eigen::MatrixXd> factorizeMomentMatrix(const Eigen::MatrixXd &M, const double *coord, int nCoveringKernels) const

Factorize the moment matrix \( \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x}) \) and check that it is regular.

checkNonSingularity() only compares the number of covering kernels with the size of the basis, which is necessary but not sufficient: for nodes in a degenerate arrangement (e.g. collinear nodes in 2D at order 1), or for a point covered by no kernel at all, \( \boldsymbol{M} \) is singular, and solving it would silently give shape functions without partition of unity.

  • coord – [in] Evaluation point (for the error message).

  • nCoveringKernels – [in] Number of kernels covering the point (for the error message).

Throws:

std::runtime_error – if M is rank deficient. A common cause in 3D is a single layer of particles through the thickness: all kernel centres are coplanar, so a linear basis cannot be reproduced; use at least two layers of kernels, larger supports, or a lower completeness order.

The column-pivoting Householder QR factorization of M.

class ReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit : public Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximation
#include <MarmotMeshfreeReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit.h>

Inheritance diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit:

Collaboration diagram for Marmot::Discretizations::Meshfree::ReproducingKernelApproximationImplicit:

Reproducing kernel approximation with implicit gradients.

The shape function values are those of ReproducingKernelApproximation. The gradients are not obtained by differentiating \( \Psi_A \) but are constructed directly as corrected kernels (implicit, or synchronized, gradients),

\[ \Psi^{(i)}_A(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}^T(\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A)\, \boldsymbol{b}^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \phi_A(\boldsymbol{x}), \qquad \boldsymbol{M}(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{b}^{(i)}(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{H}^{(i)}_0, \]
with the same moment matrix \( \boldsymbol{M} \). The right-hand side \( \boldsymbol{H}^{(i)}_0 = -\partial \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{z}) / \partial z_i |_{\boldsymbol{z} = \boldsymbol{0}} \) (the sign stems from the shifted argument \( \boldsymbol{z} = \boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{x}_A \)) is \( -1 \) at the position of the linear monomial \( z_i \) in \( \boldsymbol{H} \) and zero elsewhere (the position is found from Math::computeMonomialBasisGradient() at the origin, so it is correct for any order). This enforces the gradient reproducing conditions
\[ \sum_A \Psi^{(i)}_A(\boldsymbol{x})\, \boldsymbol{x}_A^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}{\partial x_i}, \qquad |\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le n, \]
so the implicit gradients reproduce the derivatives of all polynomials up to the completeness order, but they are not the derivatives of the values \( \Psi_A \). They require neither kernel gradients nor \( \boldsymbol{M}_{,i} \): all \( 1 + d \) right-hand sides are solved with one QR decomposition of \( \boldsymbol{M} \).

concept GeometryCellPolicy
#include <MarmotCellGeometry.h>

Requirements on the geometry policy of a cell (e.g. Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::DisplacementCell).

A geometry policy must provide the types XiSized ( \( n_\mathrm{dim} \) vector), NSized ( \( 1\times n_\mathrm{nodes} \)) and dNdXSized ( \( n_\mathrm{dim}\times n_\mathrm{nodes} \)) and the methods findReferenceCoordinate, N, dNdX and detJ with the signatures of CellGeometry. The cells additionally call isCoordinateInCell, getBoundingBox and getElementShape, which the concept does not check. Implementations: Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::LagrangianCellGeometry, Marmot::Discretizations::Cells::BSplineCellGeometry.

namespace Math

Functions

template<int p>
double B(double u, const double *knotVec, int i)

Evaluate the B-spline basis function \( N_{i,p}(u) \) by the Cox–de Boor recursion.

\[ N_{i,p}(u) = \frac{u - z_i}{z_{i+p} - z_i} N_{i,p-1}(u) + \frac{z_{i+p+1} - u}{z_{i+p+1} - z_{i+1}} N_{i+1,p-1}(u), \]
where a term is omitted ( \( 0/0 := 0 \)) if its knot difference is below \( 10^{-14} \) (repeated knots). The recursion ends at B< 0 >.

Template Parameters:

p – Degree \( p \) of the B-spline (order \( p + 1 \)).

Parameters:

  • u – [in] Parameter value \( u \).

  • knotVec – [in] Knot vector \( z \); entries \( z_i, \dots, z_{i+p+1} \) are accessed.

  • i – [in] Index \( i \) of the basis function.

Returns:

\( N_{i,p}(u) \).

template<int p>
double dB_dU(double u, const double *knotVec, int i)

Evaluate the derivative \( \mathrm{d}N_{i,p}/\mathrm{d}u \) of a B-spline basis function.

Differentiates the Cox–de Boor recursion of B() term by term,

\[ \frac{\mathrm{d}N_{i,p}}{\mathrm{d}u} = \frac{N_{i,p-1} + (u - z_i)\, N'_{i,p-1}}{z_{i+p} - z_i} + \frac{-N_{i+1,p-1} + (z_{i+p+1} - u)\, N'_{i+1,p-1}}{z_{i+p+1} - z_{i+1}}, \]
omitting terms with a knot difference below \( 10^{-14} \). The recursion ends at dB_dU< 0 > \( = 0 \).

Template Parameters:

p – Degree \( p \) of the B-spline.

Parameters:

  • u – [in] Parameter value \( u \).

  • knotVec – [in] Knot vector \( z \); entries \( z_i, \dots, z_{i+p+1} \) are accessed.

  • i – [in] Index \( i \) of the basis function.

Returns:

\( \mathrm{d}N_{i,p}/\mathrm{d}u \).

inline int computeSizeOfMonomialBasisVector(int order, int dim)

Compute the size of the complete monomial basis of a given order.

Computes the size of the H vector based on the completeness order and the dimension, cf. Eq. (3.67) in the book by Belytschko, Chen, Hillman, i.e., the number of monomials \( \boldsymbol{x}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} \) with \( |\boldsymbol{\alpha}| \le n \) in \( d \) dimensions, \( \binom{d + n}{d} \).

Parameters:

  • order – [in] Completeness order \( n \) (zero for a negative order).

  • dim – [in] Spatial dimension \( d \ge 1 \).

Returns:

The number of monomials.

inline int _computeMonomialBasisRecursion(int order, const Eigen::VectorXd &x, Eigen::VectorXd &res, int idxEnd, int dim)

Recursive kernel of computeMonomialBasis().

Multiplies the entries starting at idxEnd by the powers \( x_k^i \) of the coordinates \( k \le \) dim, for all exponent combinations of total degree \( \le \) order. The loop over the exponent of coordinate dim is the outermost one, the recursion handles the lower coordinates.

Parameters:

  • order – [in] Remaining total degree.

  • x – [in] Coordinates.

  • res – [inout] Basis vector, initialized with ones by the caller.

  • idxEnd – [in] First entry of res treated by this call.

  • dim – [in] Number of (leading) coordinates treated by this call.

Returns:

One past the last entry of res treated by this call.

inline int _computeMonomialBasisGradientRecursion(int order, const Eigen::VectorXd &x, Eigen::MatrixXd &res, int idxEnd, int dim)

Recursive kernel of computeMonomialBasisGradient().

Same traversal as _computeMonomialBasisRecursion(). By the product rule, column \( k \) of an entry is multiplied by \( \partial x_k^i / \partial x_k = i\, x_k^{i-1} \) for its own coordinate and by \( x_j^i \) for all other coordinates \( j \neq k \).

Parameters:

  • order – [in] Remaining total degree.

  • x – [in] Coordinates.

  • res – [inout] Gradient matrix (basis size \( \times d \)), initialized with ones by the caller.

  • idxEnd – [in] First row of res treated by this call.

  • dim – [in] Number of (leading) coordinates treated by this call.

Returns:

One past the last row of res treated by this call.

inline void computeMonomialBasis(int order, const Eigen::VectorXd &x, Eigen::VectorXd &res)

Evaluate the complete monomial basis \( \boldsymbol{H}(\boldsymbol{x}) \) of order \( n \).

The entries are all monomials \( x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_d^{\alpha_d} \) with \( \alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_d \le n \), ordered with the exponent of the last coordinate varying slowest and that of the first coordinate fastest. For example, in 2D with \( n = 2 \): \( \boldsymbol{H} = [1,\ x_1,\ x_1^2,\ x_2,\ x_1 x_2,\ x_2^2]^T \); in 3D with \( n = 1 \): \( \boldsymbol{H} = [1,\ x_1,\ x_2,\ x_3]^T \). The first entry is always \( 1 \).

Parameters:

  • order – [in] Completeness order \( n \).

  • x – [in] Coordinates \( \boldsymbol{x} \) (the dimension \( d \) is taken from its size).

  • res – [out] Basis vector; must already have the size computeSizeOfMonomialBasisVector( order, d ).

inline void computeMonomialBasisGradient(int order, const Eigen::VectorXd &x, Eigen::MatrixXd &res)

Evaluate the gradient \( \partial \boldsymbol{H} / \partial \boldsymbol{x} \) of the monomial basis.

Row \( k \) corresponds to entry \( k \) of computeMonomialBasis() (same ordering), column \( i \) to \( \partial / \partial x_i \).

Parameters:

  • order – [in] Completeness order \( n \).

  • x – [in] Coordinates \( \boldsymbol{x} \) (the dimension \( d \) is taken from its size).

  • res – [out] Gradient matrix; must already have the size computeSizeOfMonomialBasisVector( order, d ) \( \times d \).

Include dependency graph for MarmotBSpline.h:

This graph shows which files directly or indirectly include MarmotBSpline.h:

B-spline basis functions of arbitrary degree and their derivatives (Cox–de Boor recursion).

The functions evaluate the \( i \)-th B-spline basis function \( N_{i,p}(u) \) of degree \( p \) over a non-decreasing knot vector \( \{z_0, z_1, \dots\} \), and its derivative \( \mathrm{d}N_{i,p}/\mathrm{d}u \). The degree is a template parameter, so the recursion is resolved at compile time. They are declared in the global namespace.

Defines generic cells (Quad4, Hex8) for meshfree methods.

This file provides template classes for 2D quadrilateral (Quad4) and 3D hexahedral (Hex8) isoparametric cells. It includes functionality for shape functions, Jacobian computation, centroid, volume/area, second moments, and uniform subdivision.

The elements use Abaqus node and face numbering conventions where applicable.
